Laurence
sampled:
Tribe, a professor of constitutional law at Harvard University and a former professor of federal constitutional law, is a member of USA TODAY's Board of Contributors. Follow him on Twitter: @tribelaw.
President Donald Trump is claiming the power to pardon himself, but the Constitution says he can't. The Constitution tells us so.
Trump is asserting that he has the right to pardon himself because he is the chief executive. Presidents have this power, but they can't also do other things that violate the Constitution.
For example, presidents can't use the pardon power to block criminal prosecutions. You can't pardon yourself for a crime that hasn't been charged. Nor can you pardon yourself for a civil offense, like an unpaid parking ticket.
And that's not all: A self-pardon would violate the fundamental principle of criminal immunity. The Constitution says the president "shall have Power to grant Reprieves and Pardons for Offenses against the United States." That means no one else can pardon you, including yourself.
Trump's latest claims are part of a broad and dangerous trend. Since the Watergate scandal, presidents have sought to place themselves above the law and to rewrite the Constitution to suit their personal whims.

original: For professors, publishing in elite journals is an unavoidable part of university life. The grueling process of subjecting work to the up-or-down judgment of credentialed scholarly peers has been a cornerstone of academic culture since at least the mid-20
sampled:
th century. But as the internet has become an increasingly important source of information, and as the public’s appetite for knowledge has grown, the ways in which academics and the public have access to the fruits of their work has changed.

Over the past several years, academic publishing has become a battleground between the publishing industry and the internet. A small group of publishers has sought to keep their monopoly on the market, by introducing new fees and restrictions that have been met with fierce resistance from academics and technologists. Meanwhile, the internet has developed a suite of tools and services that make it easier than ever for people to share scholarly knowledge on a massive scale, and without the need for a middleman.

With the rise of for-profit “predatory” publishers and the “open access” movement, the traditional scholarly publishing model has come under increasing attack from academics and the public. But, despite the efforts of a small number of publishers, the scholarly publishing industry is in trouble and is facing a number of problems that threaten its very existence. In this talk, I will discuss these problems and the path forward for a more sustainable system of academic publishing.

I previously wrote an article stating that the Texas Primary Elections will likely be split with one in March and the other in May. This is what the Texas Republican Party and the AG argued for.
Not everyone likes that idea though, and there are many
sampled:
other problems with it.

The main problem is that it splits the vote and gives the more conservative candidates a much easier path to the nomination than they otherwise would have. It’s a political party, not a sports league — voters have a right to choose who represents them, not the other way around.

In a general election, there aren’t enough votes to split between two or three candidates, but in a primary, the situation is different. In a primary, the person with the most votes wins. If there were three candidates in the race, that third candidate would win with a plurality, not a majority.

The argument against a primary in May, before the general election, is that it would cause confusion and lead to a situation where the most conservative candidate wins without getting a majority of the votes.

This is not a problem with primaries in general, but rather with primaries in March.

In a general election, voters know who the candidates are and they know the issues, which is why there are debates and the general election. In a primary, the candidates are new to the voters and they have no idea what the candidates stand for or what they will stand for on the issues.
